chapter 07 · evaluation

What counts as "it worked"

You gave up a DAG you could read for a search you cannot predict. The price of that trade is that you can no longer reason about a run before it happens — so the only remaining way to know whether the thing works is to measure it. An agent without an eval is a demo, and a demo that ran once is not evidence of anything.

You already know how to do this. It is a benchmarking paper: fixed baselines, fixed seeds, paired cases, reported variance, and a stated result that would make you abandon the approach. The three things that are genuinely different are below.

01

You are not measuring a model

The unit of evaluation is the whole agent–environment system.

A capability claim is a property of a fully specified system, never of the base model alone. Change the tool description and the number moves. Change the context policy and it moves again. "Opus scores X on this task" is not a well-formed statement unless everything around it is pinned.

Freeze, and reportBecause otherwise
model and versionthe number silently changes under you
scaffold, prompts, tool registry and tool versionsyou measured a different agent last week
data snapshotthe corpus moved; the comparison is void
budgets — tokens, steps, wall-clock→ the chapter 06 confound, exactly
the graderan LLM judge is a model with a version too

Run in resettable containers, with executable checks wherever one exists. Preserve raw trajectories — when a result surprises you, the transcript is the only place the answer lives.

02

Capability and reliability are different numbers

pass@k and pass^k, and why the gap between them is the real finding.
MeansAnswers
pass@kat least one success in k independent attempts"could it ever do this?" — an oracle, best-of-k quantity
pass^kevery one of k attempts succeeds"can I deploy this?" — the reliability quantity

The number that should recalibrate you: τ-bench found state-of-the-art function-calling agents below 50% task success — and in the retail domain, pass^8 under 25%. An agent that succeeds half the time and is consistent almost never. Your working demo is a pass@k observation with k = however many times you quietly re-ran it.

How many repeats

There is no defensible universal count — it follows from the smallest effect you care about and the variance you actually observe. Two anchors, so the arithmetic is not a surprise:

5–10 rollouts per task      # reasonable minimum for screening
~96 observations            # ±10-point 95% margin at a rate near 0.5
~384 observations           # ±5-point margin

Which means a confident claim that one variant beats another by a few points, measured on one run of twenty tasks, is not supported by its own sample size. Use paired repeated rollouts for every condition, and compute uncertainty with a task-clustered bootstrap — a pooled binomial interval ignores that rollouts of the same task are correlated and will overstate your confidence.

03

Score the chain, not the conclusion

Otherwise a plausible narrative on top of an invalid pipeline scores full marks.

In a scientific domain the single most dangerous grading scheme is "did the final answer look right?" — because a fluent summary of a broken run looks exactly like a fluent summary of a good one.

  1. Input and setup validity. Right data, right reference build, QC passed. Deterministic — check it with code.
  2. Choices. Workflow and parameters appropriate for the question. This is where a defensible alternative must not be marked wrong.
  3. Execution. Tools exited cleanly and produced the artefacts — which, as ever, are two different claims.
  4. Quantitative agreement. Against a blinded reference, by a metric chosen in advance.
  5. Interpretation. Are the claims supported by the figures and logs produced, and do they state their uncertainty?

The precedent exists: a published scientific-agent benchmark scores the generated program, the execution result, and the cost separately; a biomedical one argues for expert-designed process-level rubrics, precisely because outcome-only scoring rewards memorization and rejects valid alternative analyses.

Partial credit is necessary, but it must be structured. Score independently auditable dimensions rather than one holistic "correct" label. A single blended score cannot tell you whether the agent chose well and the tool failed, or chose badly and got lucky — and those call for opposite fixes.

Two cautions about benchmarks, from the literature itself. A perturbation-based bio-agent benchmark found that superficially completed pipelines break under controlled perturbation — corrupt an input, add a decoy file, pad the prompt — so "it ran" is not "it reasoned". And an external audit of a widely used computational-biology agent benchmark argued that flawed tasks and LLM-judge errors accounted for roughly 70% of apparent failures, shifting scores by up to 42 points. A benchmark is an instrument, and instruments need calibrating too. (Both reported by the research pass; cited sources not independently verified here.)

04

Writing the protocol

Before you build the thing it judges.

Write it first. An eval designed after the agent is an eval shaped by what the agent happens to do well, and you will not notice it happening.

SectionWhat goes in it
BaselinesWhat you must beat: the existing method, the trivial method, and the agent's own ablations — no retrieval, no subagents, half the budget
CasesFixed, pre-registered, with known answers. Include ones you expect to fail
RepeatsA number justified by pilot variance, not by convenience
MetricsPer-stage, auditable, chosen before seeing results. Plus cost, wall-clock, tokens, tool calls, failures — and cost per completed task, which is the one that decides whether anyone uses it
AttributionWhich ablation separates "the agent chose well" from "the underlying tool is good"
Stopping ruleThe result that would make you abandon the approach — written down in advance, where it can still be honest

The attribution row is the one specific to agents. If an agent runs a good tool and gets a good answer, you have learned nothing about the agent. The ablation that matters is the fixed pipeline: the same tools in a sensible hand-written order, no model deciding anything. If the agent cannot beat that, you have built an expensive way to run a script — which is a fine thing to discover in week three and a terrible thing to discover in a reviewer's report.

Exercise p7 — one table you would show a reviewer. Compare two variants of your own agent, properly.

Do thisWhat it establishes
Fix cases and write the grader before running anythingthe eval cannot be tuned to the result
Run both variants n times each, paired on cases, matched budgetthe only comparison that isolates the change
Report pass@1, pass^n, and cost per completed taskcapability, reliability and whether it is affordable
Bootstrap the interval, clustered by taskwhether your difference is real
Include a fixed-pipeline ablationwhether the agency bought anything at all
Show the cases where it losesthe part that makes the rest believable

You can now write an eval protocol for an agent you built — baselines, cases, repeats, metrics, attribution, and the result that would make you stop.

That is the course. What remains is to apply it: the capstone is a real 3D-genomics agent with papers attached, where every chapter above becomes a decision someone will ask you to defend.
